Getting ready for the first birthday
14 January, evening. Tomorrow Rosa Elena turns one. Ana and Mihai are getting the party ready and remembering the past year.
Do you remember this evening a year ago? We were eating your mother’s ciorbă.
How could I forget? I still dream about that night. Well, not the part with the traffic lights.
Ha-ha. Mrs Maria still insists you went through two red lights.
Mrs Maria forgets it was nine in the evening and there was nobody about. Right, who have we invited?
Your parents, Mrs Maria, Mr Ilie, and Andrei with his father. And on video call, the whole of Madrid and Yuki.
Andrei’s father is coming? I can’t believe it.
He insisted on coming. He says he wants to meet the little girl his son talks about so much. And that I can count on him if anything in the house needs fixing.
Who’d have thought it. And the weather, what’s the forecast?
It depends on the website. One says it’ll snow, another that it’ll be sunny. My mum says it all depends on how we behave.
Typical Carmen. Hey, what are you thinking about? You’ve gone quiet.
I’m thinking about everything that’s happened this year. I fell in love with this city without realising it. And that’s even though at first I complained about everything.
Not everything. The cold, the noise, sarmale for breakfast…
OK, almost everything. But you know what? I’m glad I trusted you when you told me about Bucharest.
And I’m glad I married such a brave woman. Come on, shall we get the cake ready? The idea is to have it done before the most demanding judge in the house wakes up.
“quién lo diría” = who’d have thought it
“me enamoré de” = I fell in love with
“se trata de” = the idea is, it’s about
kon-MEE-go, kon-TEE-go: a single word. Not “con mí” or “con ti”!
a-kor-DAR-seh-deh: the preposition is linked to the verb. «¿Te acuerdas de mí?» = teh-a-KWER-das-deh-MEE.
The birthday song in Spain: «Cumpleaños feliz, te deseamos a ti, que los cumplas feliz…». koom-pleh-A-nyos feh-LEETH.
Many Spanish verbs come “packaged” with a fixed preposition, and that preposition is often different from the English one. They have to be learned together, like a single word.
When a verb follows the preposition, it’s in the INFINITIVE (where English often uses -ing): Insistió en venir. Me alegro de verte. Sueño con viajar a Japón.
When “que + another person” follows the preposition, the preposition STAYS and the subjunctive follows: Insistió en que fuéramos. Me alegro de que hayas venido.
de mí, en mí, para mí
de ti, en ti, para ti
“mí” with an accent (pronoun) versus “mi” without (possessive): para mí (for me), mi casa (my house). “ti” NEVER has an accent.
I think about you a lot.
Sin embargo, aun así, por lo tanto, además.
Se puso rojo. Se ha vuelto serio. Se hizo médico.
Pienso en ti. Sueño con viajar.

Carta para Rosa Elena, a los dieciocho años
On the evening before the birthday, Ana writes a letter for Rosa Elena to open when she turns 18. She’ll put it in the box under the floor.
Dear Rosa: when you read this letter, you’ll already have turned eighteen. I wonder what you’ll think about, what you’ll dream of, who you’ll have fallen in love with.
I don’t know if you’ll remember this house the way I see it now: with the green balcony, Mrs Maria’s cats and the smell of the acacias in spring.
What I do know is that you grew up between two languages, three cuisines and lots of people who loved you from the very first day.
A piece of advice from your mother: trust yourself. And when you depend on others, choose carefully the people you count on.
And never forget to open the window when something important happens. That’s what your father did on the day you were born. We love you, Mum.
“no te olvides de” = don’t forget to
Abrir la ventana cuando pase algo importante

On the fifteenth of January it was snowing when day broke. Not heavy snow, but the gentle kind, with big flakes falling slowly, as if they were in no hurry. Carmen, who had arrived from Madrid the night before, said it was a sign.
“I don’t know yet. But signs make sense afterwards.”
At twelve the guests began to arrive. First Mrs Maria, with a walnut cozonac and her six cats, who came in behind her as if they’d been invited too.
Then Elena and Ion, who had come from Brașov by train. Ion had a wooden box wrapped in newspaper under his arm. He wouldn’t let anyone open it.
Mr Ilie came alone, punctual as ever, with a small present: a handmade wooden stool, just the right size for a one-year-old.
Last came Andrei and his father. Mr Dan was wearing the same grey jacket as always, but this time he was smiling. Andrei was carrying a huge painting wrapped in a blanket.
At one, Mihai switched on the computer in the living room. One after another, the little squares of the video call appeared on the screen.

From Madrid, Grandma Rosario, in a party hat. From the restaurant, Kenji, Sofía, Hanako and Carlos, all singing at the same time and in different keys. From Tokyo, Yuki, with her eyes half closed because it was nine in the evening there and she had just finished work.
And from the library in Madrid, Mrs Suzuki, with Tama in her arms. The cat was eyeing the screen suspiciously.

Someone was missing. Grandpa Gheorghe. He was ninety-three, and the snow had closed the road to his village. Ion explained that he had called him in the morning and that Grandpa had insisted they shouldn’t worry about him.

It was time for the cake. Carmen had made it from Grandma Rosario’s recipe; Elena had decorated it with walnuts, Romanian style; and Kenji, on video call, had insisted on a little sugar cherry blossom.

They sat Rosa Elena on Mr Ilie’s stool, in front of the cake, with a single lit candle. The baby looked very closely at the flame. Then she looked at everyone. Then she looked at the screen, where twenty faces were singing to her in three languages.
“Blow, sweetheart,” Ana told her. “Like this: phoooo.”
Rosa Elena didn’t blow. She sat looking at the candle, very seriously, as if she were thinking about something important.
And then, in front of everyone, she said her first word.
There was silence. Then everyone started talking at once.
“No, no,” said Carmen. “She said ‘pan’ (bread). She’s pointing at the cake!”
“She said ‘pâine’,” said Elena in Romanian. “She just didn’t get to finish.”
On the screen, Yuki burst out laughing. “In Japanese, ‘pa’ is the sound of something opening suddenly. Like a flower.”
Nobody could agree. Each of them was sure the baby had said the word in their own language. In the end it was Andrei who settled the argument, as often happens with people who speak little.
“Maybe she said all three,” he said. “Daddy, bread and flower. We’re talking about a little girl with three languages. Why should she have to choose one?”
Everyone fell silent. Then Mr Dan, who hadn’t opened his mouth all afternoon, began to clap. And everyone, in Bucharest, in Madrid and in Tokyo, clapped with him.
Rosa Elena, frightened by the noise, burst into tears. And while she was crying, she blew out the candle without meaning to.
Later, after the guests had left, Ion finally opened the box wrapped in newspaper. Inside was a letter from Grandpa Gheorghe, written in large, shaky handwriting.
Mihai read it out loud and translated it for Ana and Carmen:
“Dear Rosa Elena: today I can’t be with you because the snow won’t let me. But don’t worry: we old folk learn to be in places even when we’re not there.”

“I’m leaving you a present that took me ninety years to find: patience. It can’t be wrapped. So I’m leaving you this little wooden bell, the first one I made as a boy. When it rings, remember that someone in the mountains is thinking of you.”
At the bottom of the box there was a little wooden bell, darkened by the years. Ana picked it up and shook it gently. It rang dry and warm, like an old door opening.
When she heard it, Rosa Elena, who was almost asleep, opened her eyes, reached out towards the bell and said, very slowly and very clearly, her second word:
Carmen looked at Ana. Ana looked at Mihai. And Mihai, with tears in his eyes, said what they were all thinking: “Bunicu. She’s started saying ‘bunicu’ (Grandpa).”
Outside it was still snowing, slowly, unhurriedly. Carmen went over to the window and opened it for ten seconds. Now she understood the sign.

That night, when everyone was asleep, Mihai went down to the living room. He lifted the lid in the floor and opened the wooden box. Inside were Grandma Ileana’s letter, the silver ring, the photo of the two soldiers and the neighbours’ note.
He put in the letter Ana had written for Rosa Elena. Then, carefully, he added Grandpa Gheorghe’s wooden bell.

He stayed for a while looking at the box, which was getting fuller and fuller. He thought of all the people who had touched those things: soldiers, grandparents, neighbours, carpenters. None of them had imagined that one day it would all end up together, in a box under the floor.
When he went back upstairs, he found Ana awake, sitting by the cradle. “Where were you?” she asked softly.
“Putting things away for the future,” he answered. And he sat down next to her to watch the little girl who had said three words in a single day, in three languages at once.
¿Por qué no vino el abuelo Gheorghe?
La nieve había cerrado la carretera
Según Andrei, ¿qué había dicho la niña?
Las tres cosas: papá, pan y flor

Ana: I still laugh when I remember the argument about the first word. I think Andrei was right.
I have news for you: I’ve fallen in love. His name is Takeshi and he teaches Spanish at my university. We met because he complained about my Madrid accent.
I don’t know yet if I’ll marry him. It depends on lots of things. But I’m counting on you to give me advice.
And don’t forget one thing: the club started with you and me in a library. Look at everything that’s happened since then.
